newsitem.title: USA: U.S. YIELD CURVE -- No clear signal on Fed policy.
newsitem.headline: U.S. YIELD CURVE -- No clear signal on Fed policy.

text.p: For those trying to gauge whether the U.S. Treasury market expects a rate hike by looking at the yield curve, good luck.

Players said the 65-basis-point spread between two-year notes and 30-year bonds says little. It is identical to its level day after the Federal Reserve last raised rates and the market was debating whether it would move next in May or July.
"The market is pretty confused at this point," said Dave Connors, manager of U.S. government trading at Credit Suisse First Boston. "The market is very close to 50-50 on a move.
"If you ask most people their opinion, the honest answer is, 'I don't know.' There are not too many who have a strong conviction," he added.

In April, it had looked as if the market had factored in another rate hike in May, evidenced by the flattening on the curve to 60 basis points. But remarks from Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan last Thursday triggered a steepening of about seven basis points as the market interpreted his comments to mean the Fed was on hold.

Since then, the curve narrowed about two basis points as some players felt they were too quick to de-price a tightening. Market participants gave up trying to predict what the Fed would do next week, claiming it is a toss-up.
Indeed, the June federal funds contract on Friday was at 5.61 percent, an indication that about 40 percent of the market expects a rate hike next week.
"The curve as well as funds are telling you that the market is not real certain," said Steve Slifer, chief U.S. economist at Lehman Brothers Inc. "It's not a lay-up on either side," he said.
With no key economic reports due before Tuesday's meeting, players said it was unlikely the yield curve would shift dramatically before the Fed meeting.

Neil DeSarno, head trader at CIBC Wood Gundy Securities Corp said the curve has a greater risk of flattening "as we have more people going into the camp that maybe there is a need for more insurance on Tuesday.
"The curve will continue to be choppy until Tuesday," he added.
Players said that the 0.3 percent rise in the core consumer price index in April underscored the view inflation is not down for the count.
"It gives you a sense that there is always potential for an inflation pick-up," Connors said. "We are not seeing anything worrisome, but no one can make the conclusion that there is no inflation."

Meanwhile, Friday's data showed a stronger-than-expected 2.6 percent gain in April housing starts and a jump in the University of Michigan's mid-May consumer sentiment index to a record high of 104.6.
This data pushed some fence-sitters to the rate hike camp.
No matter what the outcome on Tuesday, players said the curve will look much different than it does now.
"The spread will be 75 or 50 basis points," Connors predicted.
He and others agreed that a rate hike would bring about a 12- to 15-basis point flattening of the curve with most of the narrower spread due to a rise in short-term yields.
Should the Fed stand pat, players forsee short yields falling, consequently widening the curve.
In either case, some said they expect long bond yields to fall eventually as investors realize the spread between the 30-year bond and inflation is too high.
Currently, the spread is 440 basis points, given a 6.90 percent bond yield and 2.5 percent inflation rate.
(( -- N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1867 ))
